Israelites
IZ-ray-el-ites
n. pl.
The descendants of Israel, the name God gave Jacob at Peniel — a prince with God, one who has power with God and with men. The Authorized Version uses Israelites where it wishes to name the people as individuals rather than the nation, and Paul uses it for the covenant privileges he grieves over in Romans 9.

Biblical Definition

Israelites names the covenant people one by one. Even in Egypt, before there is a nation in any political sense, the plagues distinguish them: there was not one of the cattle of the Israelites dead (Exodus 9:7). The law binds the feast of tabernacles on them by birth — all that are Israelites born shall dwell in booths (Leviticus 23:42) — a yearly week under branches to remember that their fathers had no house. In the Gospels the word becomes a commendation from the lips of Christ Himself: Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile! (John 1:47), spoken of Nathanael, and the contrast with Jacob, whose name meant supplanter and whose life was full of guile until Peniel, is surely intended. Paul lists the privileges of the name in the passage where he says he could wish himself accursed for his kinsmen: Who are Israelites; to whom pertaineth the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the service of God, and the promises (Romans 9:4). Then he makes the distinction the whole chapter turns on: they are not all Israel, which are of Israel. The name is real, the privileges are real, and neither is salvation.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines ISRAELITE as a descendant of Israel or Jacob; a Jew. The 1828 entry treats the word as simply ethnic, which is exactly the assumption Romans 9 dismantles by distinguishing Israel after the flesh from the Israel of God.

expand to see more

ISRAELITE, n. — A descendant of Israel or Jacob; a Jew.

The name Israel was given at Peniel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed (Genesis 32:28).

The Authorized Version uses children of Israel for the nation in its corporate acts and Israelites where individuals are in view.

Paul’s three-fold challenge in 2 Corinthians 11:22 — Hebrews, Israelites, the seed of Abraham — shows the terms were distinguishable to a first-century ear.

Webster’s plain ethnic definition is correct as far as English goes; Scripture’s own usage carries a covenantal freight no dictionary entry can supply.

Key Scripture

Exodus 9:7 — "And Pharaoh sent, and, behold, there was not one of the cattle of the Israelites dead. And the heart of Pharaoh was hardened, and he did not let the people go."

Leviticus 23:42 — "Ye shall dwell in booths seven days; all that are Israelites born shall dwell in booths:"

John 1:47 — "Jesus saw Nathanael coming to him, and saith of him, Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile!"

Romans 9:4 — "Who are Israelites; to whom pertaineth the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the service of God, and the promises;"

2 Corinthians 11:22 — "Are they Hebrews? so am I. Are they Israelites? so am I. Are they the seed of Abraham? so am I."

Modern Corruption

Two errors divide the field: dispensationalism, which keeps Israel and the church permanently separate with two programmes and two peoples, and the replacement caricature that treats the promises as simply cancelled. Romans 9 through 11 refuses both.

expand to see more

Paul’s method in Romans 9 is to grant every privilege and then deny that privilege saves. Who are Israelites; to whom pertaineth the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants — he does not minimize one item. Then: they are not all Israel, which are of Israel, and he proves it from Isaac against Ishmael and Jacob against Esau, both cases of natural descent that did not carry election. Dispensational premillennialism, a nineteenth-century novelty absent from every Reformation confession, keeps the two peoples on separate tracks with separate destinies and thereby loses the one olive tree of Romans 11, into which believing Gentiles are grafted and from which unbelieving branches are broken off. There is one tree. There always was.

The opposite error, and the one the dispensationalist rightly fears, is a triumphalism that speaks of the church as though God had simply finished with Israel. Romans 11 forbids it in terms: Hath God cast away his people? God forbid, and boast not against the branches, and be not highminded, but fear. The Reformed position has room for a large ingathering of Jews — the Puritans expected one, and the Westminster divines prayed for it — without inventing a second programme of redemption. What it will not do is make ethnic descent a saving category, because he is not a Jew, which is one outwardly, and the Israelite indeed is the one in whom is no guile.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Yisra’el (H3478), he will rule as God, or one who strives with God, from sarah to contend and El, God; Greek Israelites (G2475).

expand to see more

Hebrew Yisra’el (H3478) — Israel; given at Peniel (Genesis 32:28) and confirmed at Bethel (Genesis 35:10).

Hebrew sarah (H8280) — to contend, to have power as a prince; the verb in as a prince hast thou power with God.

Hebrew Yaaqob (H3290) — Jacob; heel-catcher, supplanter — the name replaced, and the guile John 1:47 says Nathanael lacks.

Greek Israelites (G2475) — an Israelite; John 1:47, Romans 9:4, 11:1, 2 Corinthians 11:22.

Greek dolos (G1388) — guile, deceit, bait; in whom is no guile (John 1:47).

Usage

"All that are Israelites born shall dwell in booths (Leviticus 23:42) — a week each year under branches, to remember."

"Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile (John 1:47) — Christ’s commendation, and the reversal of Jacob."

"Who are Israelites; to whom pertaineth the adoption (Romans 9:4) — every privilege granted, and none of them saving."
